Developmental disability in children and young people

In 2019, approximately 317 million children and young people worldwide were living with health conditions that contribute to developmental disability. The joint WHO and UNICEF report also points to barriers in healthcare, stigma, prejudice and social exclusion.

children, adolescents and young people living with those conditions in 2019
WHO and UNICEF estimated that in 2019 approximately 317 million children and young people were living with health conditions that contribute to developmental disability.

The figure groups together children and young people with health conditions that contribute to developmental disability. The framework is broader than autism, ADHD or any other specific neurodivergent condition, so it cannot be turned into a global count of neurodivergence.
Cite ‘health conditions that contribute to developmental disability’. Do not replace that wording with ‘317 million neurodivergent children’.
This figure does not mean 317 million neurodivergent children. The framework includes a broad set of congenital or acquired conditions that may lead to developmental disability.

Why comparable developmental data are missing

Not all figures described as ‘global’ represent every region in the same way. A 2023 international review concluded that, for several developmental disabilities, geographical coverage was insufficient and methods were too heterogeneous for the estimates to be considered fully representative of the planet.

The figures
A 2023 umbrella review examined global estimates for ADHD, autism, cerebral palsy, developmental intellectual disability, epilepsy, hearing loss, visual loss and dyslexia.
Its conclusion is important for the Data tab:
> Many estimates labelled as ‘global’ come from samples concentrated in high-income countries and show substantial methodological heterogeneity.

This page does not count a population: it assesses how representative the available evidence is. The review shows that a figure called global may rely mainly on studies from high-income countries and on methods that differ widely from one another.
This page does not provide a prevalence estimate: it documents a limitation in the global evidence. It should be cited as a methodological warning.
The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

ADHD in children and adolescents

An international umbrella review bringing together 588 studies and more than 3.27 million participants estimated a pooled ADHD prevalence of 8.0% in children and adolescents. The figure was 10% in boys and 5% in girls.
